newsitem.title: UK: Maggots munch wounds clean, plastic surgeon says.
newsitem.headline: Maggots munch wounds clean, plastic surgeon says.

text.p: Maggots that thrive on dead body tissue could be the latest weapon for plastic surgeons trying to save a patient's limb, a British doctor said on Tuesday.

Kenneth Graham, a plastic surgeon at University College Hospital in London, said he had used maggots to heal up badly infected wounds in six patients -- with a little tickling sensation the only side-effect.

Graham told a meeting of the British Association of Plastic Surgeon the maggots had several beneficial effects. They secrete an enzyme that breaks down dead tissue as they feast. Fluid that builds up in the wound washes away bacteria.
He said the maggots also create alkaline conditions which are conducive to healing.
Graham said patients do not have to spend any time in surgery or in a hospital room.
One patient was "walking down Oxford Street" in London hours after treatment, with the maggots quietly doing their work as he shopped, Graham said.

Graham described three patients he had successfully treated. One had bedsores after a long illness. Another had an infected wound from surgery and a third had ulcers related to heart disease and diabetes.
All had infections that months of antibiotic treatment had failed to clear up. One alternative would have been radical surgery -- amputation or large-scale removal of affected area.

But the maggots cleaned up the wounds in days or weeks. "You can see all the dead tissue is gone and you have nice, red tissue. Everything is nice and clean in six weeks -- and the patient had had the wound for six months. That is remarkable," Graham told a news conference after the meeting.
The maggots are washed into a piece of plastic mesh, which is placed over the wound. The dressing is then sealed.
He said 100 maggots would eat between 10 and 15 grams (0.3 to 0.5 ounces) of dead flesh a day. The two mm (0.08 inch) long maggots grow 10 to 20 times.
Grahamsaid his group had developed a method for suctioning the maggots out when work was done. "There is no question of them burrowing into the wound and being difficult to get out."
A skin graft can disguise the hole left by the infection.

Graham got his maggots from Britain's National Health Service's Surgical Materials Testing Laboratory in Bridgend, Wales. The lab takes eggs from a species of blowfly known as a greenbottle fly and sterilises them before hatching the maggots.
Each bottle of 150-200 maggots cost 36 pounds sterling ($60) and treatment was cheap because patients needed less care.
Graham said more research was needed to find out if the maggots produced chemicals that could be isolated.
"We may be able to extract things from the maggots and not use the maggots at all." REUTER
